sources.claim: The Cloud Run container file system is in memory, so writing to it uses the instance's memory, and data written there does not persist when the instance stops. An instance whose containers exceed the total memory limit is terminated, and requests still processing on it end with HTTP 500.

Instance memory must cover the process's own allocations and files written to the file system; instances that exceed their memory limit are terminated. The 512 MiB default does not apply here: the synthetic revision states an explicit 1 GiB limit, which outranks the stale runbook figure.

Files written to disk consume memory, can persist between invocations on a reused instance, and can eventually cause an out-of-memory error if not deleted; service state cannot be assumed to survive between requests.

Under 'Container instances exceed memory limits', files written to the local file system count toward available memory, and related errors appear in varlog/system. Google documents a request-level termination message, but not the varlog/system termination text; the fixture paraphrases it and no conclusion depends on its wording.

Cloud Run service logs use resource type cloud_run_revision with service_name, revision_name and location labels, and platform system logs are written to varlog/system. The per-instance heap and /tmp report and the job-ledger extract are authored application observations, not Cloud Run platform metrics.

a.conclusion: Release 3.6.0 retains render scratch files in /tmp/render after their uploads commit. On the terminated instances that file growth (about 600 MiB on i-7f3a) plus a stable heap of about 320 MiB reaches the revision's 1 GiB limit, so retained temporary files contribute to the memory-limit terminations. The retained files sampled are disposable copies of committed statements; the 7 jobs that ended with HTTP 500 are unreconciled. The responsible code change is not confirmed.
